claims.text: Annealing as-received Q235 steel at 700–900 °C can promote formation of an adherent, coherent oxide layer.
An adherent, coherent oxide layer formed by annealing protects Q235 steel against aggressive salt corrosion.
Annealing conditions that produce a porous or brittle oxide scale enhance corrosion degradation of Q235 steel.
Thermal annealing induces oxidation of the Q235 steel surface.
The microstructure and integrity of the surface oxide mediate Q235 steel's resistance to corrosive salt attack.
A dense, coherent oxide layer acts as a transport barrier that slows corrosion.
A porous oxide layer permits accelerated corrosive degradation.
The proposed protective oxide may be an Fe3O4/spinel layer.
Q235 samples bearing a dense, adherent oxide layer will show lower mass change than unannealed samples.
Q235 samples bearing a dense, adherent oxide layer will show lower mass change than samples bearing a porous oxide layer.
Q235 samples bearing a dense, adherent oxide layer will retain greater hardness than unannealed or porous-oxide samples after salt exposure.
Q235 samples bearing a dense, adherent oxide layer will exhibit greater wear resistance than unannealed or porous-oxide samples after salt exposure.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply during aggressive-salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially different salt chemistries because oxidation kinetics can vary.
